note: PRISMA review of 159 studies across sectors, the broadest single sweep of GenAI productivity evidence.
title: Enhancing Work Productivity through Generative Artificial Intelligence: A Comprehensive Literature Review

reading.body:
A systematic review of 159 studies across sectors finds that generative AI tools deliver genuine productivity gains at work, with adoption momentum accelerating and ChatGPT as the dominant implementation.

The evidence base for GenAI productivity is now broad enough to show a genuine pattern rather than isolated cases. Studies span education, agriculture, government, and other sectors, suggesting the technology is genuinely useful across different kinds of work rather than optimized for one domain. The concentration on conversational agents and chatbots points to where the productivity gains are actually clustering in practice.

The acceleration in research itself matters for understanding adoption trajectory. The field is not stabilizing into a mature baseline but growing in volume and breadth of investigation. This signals that organizations are still in early implementation phases and learning what these systems can do within their specific constraints and workflows.

What the data does not cover: whether productivity gains persist over time, what the actual compute and power costs are per unit of productivity gain, or how gains distribute across worker roles and skill levels. The review examines what research has documented so far, not whether current implementations are sustainable at scale or what infrastructure requirements they impose. That gap remains critical for understanding whether GenAI productivity is durable or whether it trades near-term gains for mounting resource demands downstream.

explain_beginner: Instead of running a new study, this paper asks what the existing research, taken as a whole, actually says about generative AI's effect on work productivity across different industries, and how that body of research itself has been growing and clustering. The authors systematically gathered published studies on generative AI and productivity, filtered them down using a standard review protocol, and then used citation and keyword mapping software to see which topics and authors were connected to which. This kind of stock taking mattered because the volume of writing about generative AI at work exploded very suddenly after ChatGPT's public release, and it became hard for anyone to know what the accumulated evidence actually showed versus what was just repeated commentary. The review found consistent productivity benefits reported across eight different sectors, from healthcare to engineering to business management, mainly through task automation, faster data analysis, and more personalized services. It also found the research itself was oddly disconnected, with authors mostly publishing in isolation rather than collaborating across institutions, and it does not claim that any of the underlying studies used rigorous causal methods, since a literature review inherits the limitations of the papers it summarizes.
explain_business: For a leadership team trying to figure out where generative AI is already showing productivity value across a large organization, this review's main use is as a sector map, it names eight sectors, including healthcare, engineering, business management, and government, where published evidence already points to gains from automation, faster analysis, and personalized service delivery, useful for benchmarking where a company's own pilot programs sit relative to the broader field. The gap the authors highlight, that finance applications and bias or privacy safeguards were comparatively underexplored in the literature at the time, is itself a signal, meaning less external published guidance exists for those areas and a company moving into them should expect to rely more on internal testing than on established best practice. Since this is a synthesis of already published, mostly early stage studies rather than an evaluation of any specific vendor or product, it does not translate into a dollar figure or a specific tool recommendation. It is most useful right now as a starting orientation document for identifying which industries have accumulated the most public evidence of productivity gains, with the caveat that accumulated evidence is not the same as high quality evidence, since the review does not filter by methodological rigor.
explain_practitioner: This is a PRISMA guided systematic review combined with a bibliometric analysis. The authors searched Scopus, retrieved 683 initial publications spanning 1989 through September 2023, and after screening for relevance and removing duplicates arrived at 159 papers, concentrated mostly in 2014 through 2023 with a sharp spike after late 2022. They used VOSviewer software to map co-occurrence of keywords, author collaboration networks, and geographic distribution of the research, then grouped the content thematically across eight sectors including academia, engineering, healthcare, government, and business management. Reported productivity mechanisms across these sectors centered on task automation, improved data analysis, decision support, and service personalization. The bibliometric mapping surfaced a structural gap the authors treat as a real finding in its own right, research collaboration networks were sparse, meaning most authors published in relative isolation rather than building cross institutional teams, and specific areas including finance sector applications, bias reduction methods, data privacy frameworks, and rural technology access remained comparatively underexplored across the 159 papers reviewed. Because it synthesizes existing literature rather than running new experiments, the review's conclusions are only as rigorous as the underlying studies, many of which were early stage or exploratory given how recently the technology had been released.
